clinicalPearls: A rare sporadic osteomalacia that characteristically affects the axial skeleton (spine and pelvis) while largely sparing the appendicular skeleton
Typically presents in middle-aged or older men with chronic, dull axial (usually cervical or lumbar) pain that is often mild relative to the imaging findings
Radiographs show a coarsened, disorganised trabecular pattern in the spine and pelvis resembling a coarse trabeculation, without the diffuse deformity of generalised osteomalacia
In contrast to classic osteomalacia, serum calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D metabolites are typically normal, so it is not a deficiency state
Alkaline phosphatase may be normal or mildly elevated, and there are no Looser zones or widespread fractures
Bone biopsy confirms osteomalacia with excess unmineralised osteoid, distinguishing it from other coarse-trabecular osteopathies
The course is usually benign and non-progressive, so management is largely reassurance and symptomatic analgesia rather than the vitamin D and phosphate used in deficiency osteomalacia
reference.pathophysiology: Axial osteomalacia is a mineralisation defect confined mainly to the axial skeleton, in which osteoblasts produce osteoid that mineralises slowly, leaving excess unmineralised matrix demonstrable on undecalcified bone biopsy with tetracycline labelling. Unlike the common forms of osteomalacia, it is not caused by vitamin D deficiency, phosphate wasting, or hypophosphatasia, and the mineral-regulating biochemistry is characteristically normal. The underlying cause is unknown, and it appears to reflect an intrinsic, possibly localised osteoblast dysfunction rather than a systemic hormonal abnormality. Because mineral homeostasis is intact, the disease tends to remain limited and stable, producing the coarse axial trabecular pattern and modest symptoms without the progressive deformity and fractures of systemic osteomalacia.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin D or phosphate deficiency osteomalacia
Paget disease of the spine or pelvis
Ankylosing spondylitis or other inflammatory spondyloarthropathy
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the spine and pelvis showing coarse trabeculation with axial predominance
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone (usually normal)
Vitamin D metabolites to exclude deficiency osteomalacia
Bone biopsy demonstrating osteomalacic excess osteoid where confirmation is needed
Protein electrophoresis to exclude myeloma when the pattern is atypical
Bone scintigraphy or cross-sectional imaging to distinguish from Paget disease and metastases
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or severe pain out of keeping with the usually benign course
New neurological deficit suggesting an alternative spinal pathology
Biochemical abnormalities pointing to a treatable systemic osteomalacia instead
Features suggesting malignancy or Paget disease rather than axial osteomalacia
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally benign and non-progressive, with stable symptoms over long follow-up; because it does not stem from a correctable deficiency, expectations should focus on symptom control rather than radiographic reversal.
pitfalls: Treating with vitamin D and phosphate as though it were deficiency osteomalacia, which is ineffective here
Misreading the coarse axial trabeculae as Paget disease or metastatic infiltration
Overlooking the normal mineral biochemistry that separates it from systemic osteomalacia
Escalating investigation or therapy for what is usually a stable, benign disorder
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: No specific corrective therapy exists, so management centres on symptom control with simple analgesia for the axial cervical or lumbar pain
Confirm the patient is vitamin D and calcium replete and treat any coexisting deficiency osteomalacia, while recognising this will not reverse the intrinsic mineralisation defect
Use physiotherapy, postural advice and a graded exercise programme to help axial symptoms
Reassure the patient that the condition is benign and non-progressive, framing expectations around symptom control rather than radiographic improvement
Review periodically to confirm biochemical and clinical stability
Re-investigate to exclude mimics such as myeloma, Paget disease or metastases if symptoms or imaging change
